titleEn: Nations have come into Your inheritance
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Thirteen verses of communal lament attributed to Asaph, spoken after the sanctuary has been sacked and while the dead are still lying unburied. The shape is the standard one for this kind of psalm: report of the disaster, the question how long, a demand for justice, a petition, and a vow of praise at the end. Verses 6 and 7 are the Shefoch Chamatcha of the Passover seder, said with the door open. Watch how the enemy is handled grammatically: always a plural they, never named, never given a king.

stichs.en: A psalm of Asaph.
O God, nations have come into Your inheritance;
they have defiled Your holy temple;
they have made Jerusalem into heaps of rubble.

verses.summary: The lament opens with the fact and no framing: a foreign army inside the sanctuary. Three verbs land in a row with no conjunction between them, came, defiled, made, which is how Hebrew reports a sequence at speed.

stichs.en: They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the sky,
the flesh of Your faithful ones to the beasts of the earth.

verses.summary: The desecration moves from the building to the body. The word for the faithful ones is built on the root of chesed, so the dead are named here by the covenant loyalty they kept, not by their tribe or their rank.

stichs.en: They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem,
and there is no one burying them.

verses.summary: Blood like water is not only a figure for quantity. Water is what you pour out without collecting it again. The unburied dead are the second half of the horror, and in Israelite terms the worse half.

stichs.en: We have become a reproach to our neighbours,
mockery and derision to those around us.

verses.summary: The view turns from the dead to the survivors. What the survivors suffer is not physical: it is being watched. Three nouns for contempt pile up in the second half with no verb to carry them.

stichs.en: How long, O LORD, will You be angry? Forever?
Will Your jealousy burn like fire?

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. Everything before it is report and everything after it is petition, and between the two stands the question that nearly every communal lament in the book asks in these two words.

stichs.en: Pour out Your wrath on the nations that have not known You,
and on kingdoms that have not called on Your name.

verses.summary: The imprecation, and it is addressed to God as a request rather than performed by the speaker. That distinction is the point: vengeance is handed over instead of taken.

stichs.en: For he has devoured Jacob,
and they have laid waste his dwelling place.

verses.summary: The reason clause for verse 6. The verb for devouring is singular while the verb for laying waste is plural, so one sentence holds both the individual invader and the collective enemy.

stichs.en: Do not hold the iniquities of former generations against us;
let Your mercies come quickly to meet us,
for we are brought very low.

glosses: let them come to meet us
verses.summary: The turn to Israel's own account. Guilt is not denied, and the request is about speed: let the mercies arrive before the reckoning does.

stichs.en: Help us, God of our salvation, for the sake of the glory of Your name;
and rescue us, and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name.

verses.summary: The centre of the petition and the argument that carries the psalm. The ground of rescue is named twice, and both times it is Your name rather than our worth.

stichs.en: Why should the nations say, Where is their God?
Let the avenging of Your servants' spilled blood be known among the nations, before our eyes.

verses.summary: The taunt of the nations is turned into leverage. If Israel is finished, the question Where is their God is left standing unanswered, so the psalm makes God's reputation the stake in the case.

stichs.en: Let the groaning of the prisoner come before You;
by the greatness of Your arm, leave alive those marked for death.

verses.summary: From nations back to single bodies. The prisoner groans, and what is asked is not comfort but survival: the ones already assigned to death are to be left over.

stichs.en: And return sevenfold into the bosom of our neighbours
their reproach, with which they reproached You, my Lord.

verses.summary: The one request for retaliation, and it is measured rather than open ended. Into the bosom is the image of payment dropped into the fold of a garment, and the insult being repaid is the one aimed at God.

stichs.en: And we, Your people and the flock of Your pasture,
will give You thanks forever;
generation after generation we will recount Your praise.

verses.summary: The vow that closes almost every lament. Nothing in the situation has changed by the last verse. What changes is that the speaker commits to a future in which there is something left to tell.

pardes.body: The psalm divides cleanly. Verses 1 to 4 report what happened, in finished verbs and with almost no adjectives: they came, they defiled, they made, they gave, they poured out. Verse 5 asks how long. Verses 6 and 7 ask for the wrath to be redirected. Verses 8 to 12 are the petition proper, and verse 13 is the vow of praise. Note that the temple appears once, in verse 1, and is then dropped. What the rest of the psalm is about is people: servants, faithful ones, neighbours, prisoners, us.

Verses 6 and 7 stand almost word for word in Jeremiah 10:25, where the verbs of verse 7 are plural throughout. Here {{7.1}} is singular and {{7.6}} is plural inside one sentence. Whether that is a scribal slip or a deliberate collapse of the invading army into a single devourer is disputed, and the psalm gives no way to decide. The word {{2.8}}, built on the root of chesed, is the term a later generation took as a group name, and 1 Maccabees 7:17 quotes verses 2 and 3 of this psalm over the bodies of the Hasideans killed under Alcimus.

{{6.0}}, pour out, opens the passage said at the seder when the door is opened. Its position in the evening is deliberate: it falls after the grace after meals and before the rest of Hallel, so the harshest lines in the Haggadah sit between an act of hospitality and a song of praise. The date of the psalm is itself disputed. Read one way, verse 1 is the Babylonian destruction of 586 BCE and the temple is Solomon's. Read another way, the desecration is the Seleucid one, and the psalm and the book of Maccabees are near contemporaries rather than old text and later citation. The psalm names no king and no empire, so nothing in it settles the question.

The argument of verse 9 is made twice inside a single verse: help us for the sake of the glory of {{9.6}}, and atone for the sake of {{9.6}}. Nothing at all is claimed for Israel's merit. In the mystical reading the name is not a label but the aspect of God turned toward the world, so a ruined sanctuary and a mocked people register as damage to the name itself, and repairing one is repairing the other. Verse 12 then reads as more than revenge: what is to be returned {{12.2}} is specified as the reproach aimed at God, not the one aimed at us.
